text: Chapter 1 opened with why security engineering starts with identity. This lesson gets concrete: what an identity provider actually is, real examples enterprises run on, and why identity now operates as its own plane of infrastructure other security controls depend on.

An identity provider, or IdP, is the centralized system of record an organization points everything else at. Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, and Ping Identity are real, widely used examples — each authenticates users, holds the authoritative directory of who they are, and issues the tokens or assertions downstream applications trust instead of running their own login and password store. Once an app trusts the IdP, the app itself stops deciding who can sign in.

That's why identity now functions as its own plane, not just one app among many — the same way a network has a control plane other systems constantly query. Conditional Access evaluates signals like device health and location at the IdP before access is granted. Zero Trust's 'verify explicitly' principle depends on that same IdP signal being trustworthy on every request, not just the first one. Single sign-on means every connected app trusts the IdP's decision instead of checking a password itself.

That dependency shows up directly in how Conditional Access is actually configured: a policy like this one requires MFA for every Global Administrator sign-in, across every connected application, evaluated at the IdP before any app is ever reached. Get a policy like this wrong — or skip it — and every app downstream inherits that gap, because none of them are checking for themselves.

Lesson 3 goes one level deeper: the two real protocols — SAML and OIDC — that actually carry an IdP's decision to a downstream application as a trusted sign-in, how each one's login flow actually works step by step, and why most enterprise IdPs support both at once instead of picking just one.
